slides.text: In 1970, a pavilion at the world’s fair in Osaka hid inside a cloud of its own making.
Pepsi, the soft-drink company, had handed the building to a group of American and Japanese artists and engineers.
The artist Fujiko Nakaya wrapped the dome in fog, sprayed from about 2,500 tiny nozzles.
Inside, a mirror of Mylar 90 feet across curved overhead, held in place by a vacuum.
Visitors looked up and saw themselves hanging upside down, like holograms.
Underfoot, the floor changed from stone to wood to carpet to plastic grass, and the grass played birdsong.
Not long after the fair opened, Pepsi ended the artists’ program and put on a soundtrack of its own.
Nakaya kept working with fog. Since 1998, one of her fog sculptures has rolled across a pool beside the Guggenheim in Bilbao.
